records.reference: Brown, LeMay and Bursten, Chemistry: The Central Science (solubility rules; limescale from hard water)
records.why: The draft said calcium carbonate is used to 'soften maize' in a traditional 'togwa' process. Togwa is a fermented porridge drink and does not use calcium carbonate (softening maize with lime is a different, Central American process), so the example was not sound. Kettle or pot scale is CaCO3, is familiar in Kenyan homes, and still gives the same contrast with table salt, so the lessons that say 'calcium carbonate does not dissolve' stay true. Checked: CaCO3 is insoluble in water (Lesson 2 data).

records.value: Distribute the Frayer Model organiser. Say: 'I am going to give you three new vocabulary words. Your job — with your partner — is to build the meaning of each word using your experimental data. Do NOT copy from a textbook. Use your OWN data as your evidence.' Allow 5 minutes for pairs to complete Frayer Models. Circulate; if a pair cannot define 'deliquescent', prompt: 'Which sample dissolved in the water it absorbed? What does that tell you about how strongly it attracts water?' After 8 minutes, cold-call 3 pairs to share their definition of one term each. Write the class-agreed definitions on the board. Then say: 'Now write your own explanation — alone, no partner — for why each sample behaved the way it did. Use the word because and refer to your data.' Allow 4 minutes. Cold-call 4 individual learners to read their explanation for one sample. After each reading, ask the class: 'Do you agree? What would you add or change?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds. Introduce the balanced equation for efflorescence: write Na₂CO₃·10H₂O → Na₂CO₃·H₂O + 9H₂O on the board and ask: 'What type of change is this — physical or chemical? How do you know?' WAIT TIME 12 seconds, cold-call 3 learners. Then say: 'Now make the connection. Complete this sentence in your notebook: The CAN fertiliser clumped because..., the washing soda crusted because..., and the table salt was unchanged because...' Allow 3 minutes, then cold-call 3 learners to share complete sentences. Then give this explanation in your own words (about 2 minutes), because learners will ask why the same kind of air made the fertiliser gain water but the washing soda lose water: 'Air always holds some water vapour. Each salt has its own balance with it. Calcium chloride and the ammonium nitrate in CAN pull water vapour in even from moderately humid air. Washing soda crystals hold their water loosely, so when the air holds less water vapour than the crystals give off, water leaves them. Table salt only pulls water in when the air is very humid (above about 75% relative humidity), which can happen at the coast on rainy days. So the result depends on the salt AND on the humidity of the air that day.'
records.group_headline: Nothing explained how the same ordinary air can make CAN gain water yet washing soda lose water. Added a short 'each salt has its own balance with water vapour in the air' explanation, removed the 'same air'/'dry air' contradictions, and made the answers consistent.
records.reference: Brown, LeMay and Bursten, Chemistry: The Central Science (hydrates, vapour pressure and efflorescence/deliquescence; solubility rules); Greenspan (1977), Humidity Fixed Points of Binary Saturated Aqueous Solutions, J. Res. National Bureau of Standards 81A (sodium chloride deliquesces above about 75% relative humidity)
records.why: Lesson 6 tells learners CAN took water from 'humid' air and washing soda lost water to 'dry' air, but the Unit says it was ordinary air and learners will ask how one air does both. The real reason is that every salt or hydrate has its own equilibrium with water vapour (hydrates lose water when the air holds less water vapour than their own vapour pressure; deliquescent salts gain water above their critical humidity). Added that in plain words and, for the same lesson, trimmed the Frayer (8 to 5 min), explanation (6 to 4 min) and sentence (4 to 3 min) times so the Explain phase fits its 18-minute share of the 80-minute period (see the timing group). Checked: sodium chloride's critical relative humidity is about 75% (Greenspan 1977).

records.old: Efflorescent salts like washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) lose water of crystallisation in dry air, forming a white powdery crust — this is why it is effective as a laundry water softener but must be stored in airtight containers.
records.new: Efflorescent salts like washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) lose water of crystallisation to air that holds less water vapour than the crystals give off, forming a white powdery crust, so it must be stored in airtight containers. It softens laundry water for a different reason: its carbonate ions precipitate Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions as insoluble carbonates.
records.group_headline: Lesson 7 said efflorescence is why washing soda softens water. It is not: softening is the carbonate precipitating calcium and magnesium (the Lesson 5 idea). Reading text, group prompt, summary and Final Explanation now say so.
records.reference: Brown, LeMay and Bursten, Chemistry: The Central Science (hydrates, vapour pressure and efflorescence/deliquescence; solubility rules) (hard water and precipitation of CaCO3/MgCO3 by carbonate ions)
records.why: Audit claim verified for Lesson 7 (the Final Explanation itself already gives the correct reason). Efflorescence only explains why the washing soda must be stored in a closed container. Checked by Ca(2+) + CO3(2-) -> CaCO3(s): charges 2+ and 2- cancel, one of each.

Washing soda is efflorescent: the crystals lose water of crystallisation to the air, so they shrank and formed a white powdery crust: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O → Na₂CO₃·H₂O + 9H₂O (the white powder is the monohydrate). records.new: (c) CAN fertiliser is deliquescent: the ammonium nitrate in it attracts water molecules from the humid storeroom air (calcium chloride was our model for this in the experiment), so the granules became wet and sticky and clumped together. Washing soda is efflorescent: the crystals lose water of crystallisation to the air, so they shrank and formed a white powdery crust: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O(s) → Na₂CO₃·H₂O(s) + 9H₂O(g) (the white powder is the monohydrate). The fertiliser gained water while the washing soda lost it because each salt has its own balance with the water vapour in the air: the washing soda crystals hold their water loosely and give it up when the air holds less water vapour than they give off. Table salt is not affected by water in the air at everyday humidity (it only takes up water when the air is very humid, above about 75% relative humidity), so it stayed unchanged.
records.reference: Brown, LeMay and Bursten, Chemistry: The Central Science (hydrates, vapour pressure and efflorescence/deliquescence; solubility rules); Greenspan (1977), J. Res. National Bureau of Standards 81A
